opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd say Q-LEACE is a partial success, and I want to be careful not to oversell it.

The motivation is that standard LEACE gives you a guarantee, but only against linear adversaries. It ensures the class-conditional means are equal, so no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor at recovering the concept. A neural network isn't a linear classifier, though. So the natural next step was to go one order higher and make the class-conditional covariances match as well. That's the quadratic version. If the first and second moments are identical across classes, then a whole family of simple quadratic detectors also loses its signal.

What we found is that it does make the concept noticeably harder to learn in some settings. You can see it in the learning curves: the network takes longer to pick the concept back up. But it doesn't make it impossible. A sufficiently expressive network can still find the information in higher-order statistics. So there's no "this concept is gone" guarantee the way there is in the linear case.

There's also a subtlety that surprised us. Moment matching in closed form isn't always a gentle edit to the representation. In some cases, enforcing equal covariances can introduce artifacts, and a deep network can actually exploit those, which can make the concept easier to recover than with plain linear erasure. That was a humbling result. It's an example of how an intervention that looks principled from a statistics standpoint can interact strangely with what a nonlinear learner picks up on.

So my overall assessment is that it's an interesting tool and a useful probe of how information is encoded. It tells us something about how much of a concept lives in low-order moments versus higher-order structure. But if your goal is robust, adversarially guaranteed erasure against arbitrary networks, Q-LEACE isn't that. I'm fairly skeptical anything cheap and closed-form could be, because full nonlinear erasure is basically equivalent to making the distributions identical. At that point you're often destroying a lot of other useful information too.

r001.rationale: It says matching first and second moments still leaves higher-order statistics that a sufficiently expressive network can use to recover the concept.

r002.rationale: It states that equalizing class-conditional means and covariances removes the signal for a family of simple quadratic detectors.

r003.rationale: It does not mention CIFAR-10, small classifiers, hyperparameter tuning, or the reported experiment.

r004.rationale: It does not state that Q-LEACE requires knowing the concept value at inference time.

r005.rationale: It does not attribute higher-order label leakage to a label-dependent choice of transformation.

r006.rationale: It says covariance-matching artifacts can let a deep network recover the concept more easily than after plain linear erasure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Q-LEACE is a natural extension of the LEACE work. With LEACE, the idea was: what's the smallest edit you can make to your representations, in a least-squares sense, so that no linear classifier can recover a concept better than chance? And it turns out there's a closed-form answer. You basically just need to make the class-conditional means all equal, and you can do that with a very surgical projection.

Q-LEACE asks the same question one level up. What's the minimal edit that defeats any quadratic classifier? And now you also need to match the class-conditional covariances, not just the means. We do that with optimal transport between Gaussians, so each class gets mapped onto a shared target distribution in a way that moves the data as little as possible. It's still closed-form, which I like a lot. There's no adversarial training loop, no hyperparameters to fiddle with, and you get a guarantee against a whole class of adversaries rather than just the particular one you happened to train.

Now, how well does it actually work for making concepts hard for neural networks to learn? I'd say honestly, modestly. We tried this in the data-hardening setting, where you erase a concept from the inputs, say the class label in CIFAR, and then train a network from scratch and see whether it learns the label more slowly. And what you see is that it clearly slows things down early in training. LEACE alone buys you a little, Q-LEACE buys you more. The loss curve starts higher and stays higher for a while. But the network catches up. Deep nets are perfectly happy to use third- and fourth-order statistics, texture, local structure, all the stuff that a quadratic adversary can't see, and once they find those features the concept comes right back.

So the way I'd frame it is: Q-LEACE is a very good tool for asking what kind of information a network is relying on. If erasing the first two moments barely changes anything, that tells you the concept is living in higher-order structure. That's a real scientific finding. But as a mechanism for preventing a model from learning something, it's more of a speed bump than a wall. You'd need to go to higher moments, or to some nonlinear erasure, and at that point you start destroying so much of the data that it's not obvious you're preserving anything useful anymore. There's a fundamental tension there between how much you erase and how much of the original signal you keep.

The other thing I'd flag is distortion. The quadratic version necessarily moves the data more than the linear one, because you're changing covariance structure, not just shifting means. On images that's visible. You get artifacts. So even in the regime where it works, you're paying for it in the quality of the representations you're left with.

So my overall assessment is that it's elegant, it's principled, and it's the right thing to reach for if you specifically care about quadratic adversaries. But I wouldn't oversell it as a general method for making neural networks unable to learn a concept. For that problem I think the honest answer is that we don't have a good solution yet.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish making a concept harder to read out from making it harder to learn. Those are different claims. You can remove information that’s accessible to a particular class of probes, and that can be useful, but a neural network may still recover the concept through nonlinear features or learn a different representation during training.

So I’d assess Q-LEACE empirically: after you apply it, how much additional data or compute does a fresh model need to learn the concept? Does the effect persist across architectures and training procedures? And how much unrelated information have you damaged in the process?

If a simple probe fails, that’s evidence about that probe’s access to the information. It’s not, by itself, evidence that the concept has become fundamentally difficult for neural networks to learn.

r002.rationale: It does not mention equalizing class means and covariance matrices or the resulting limitation on quadratic classifiers.

r003.rationale: It does not report Belrose's unpublished CIFAR-10 experiments, small classifiers, or hyperparameter tuning.

r004.rationale: It does not state that applying Q-LEACE requires knowing the target concept value at inference time.

r005.rationale: It does not attribute higher-order label leakage to Q-LEACE's label-dependent transformation choice.

r006.rationale: It suggests nonlinear models may recover the concept, but does not say Q-LEACE can make it easier for sufficiently deep classifiers to learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an interesting approach, but I’d distinguish removing information from making information harder to learn. LEACE gives you a fairly precise guarantee about linear predictors, and Q-LEACE extends that idea to quadratic predictors. That’s useful, because a concept can be invisible to a linear probe and still be accessible through fairly simple nonlinear structure.

But that guarantee is relative to a particular class of predictors. A neural network can potentially learn higher-order features, or find some other correlated signal that survives the intervention. So I wouldn’t interpret success against a quadratic probe as showing that the network can’t learn the concept.

The interesting empirical question is whether it actually increases the amount of data or computation needed to learn it. You’d want to train fresh models on the modified data and measure their learning curves. If they consistently need more examples, that’s evidence you’ve made the concept harder to learn—even if you haven’t made it impossible.

r001.rationale: It says a concept can be invisible to a linear probe yet accessible through simple nonlinear structure, and that neural networks may learn higher-order features.

r004.rationale: It does not mention needing the target concept's value at inference time.

r005.rationale: It does not attribute higher-order label leakage to Q-LEACE's label-dependent transformation choice.

r006.rationale: It warns that networks may learn higher-order features, but does not say Q-LEACE can make the concept easier for sufficiently deep classifiers to learn.
